Conjunctive adverb: semicolon or period on the correct side, comma on the other
Colon after a complete clause before an explanation or specified item
No punctuation with a restrictive clause or restrictive appositive
Comma plus coordinating conjunction between independent clauses
Dash pair around a supplementary element
Comma before a trailing nonrestrictive modifier
Colon between independent clauses (second explains first)
Comma or parenthesis pair around a supplementary element

Question versus statement (word order and end mark)
Items in a series (commas; semicolons when items contain commas)

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses: period before a past-participle opener
items.passage: Agnes Denes, a Hungarian-born American conceptual artist, created one of her most celebrated installations in 1982 on a vacant Manhattan ______ of construction debris and planted with wheat by Denes and a few volunteers, two acres of the site eventually yielded more than 1,000 pounds of grain.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Agnes Denes ... created one of her most celebrated installations in 1982 on a vacant Manhattan landfill” is a complete sentence. “Cleared of construction debris and planted with wheat by Denes and a few volunteers” describes the subject of the next sentence, “two acres of the site,” which has its own verb, “yielded.” A period is needed between the two independent clauses.

A.recipe: comma splice (opener read as a modifier of clause 1's last noun)
A.why_wrong: The comma makes “cleared of construction debris ...” look like a description of “landfill,” but “two acres of the site eventually yielded ...” is a second independent clause, so the two clauses end up joined with only a comma.

B.why_wrong: With no punctuation, “landfill cleared of construction debris ...” attaches the phrase to the first clause, and the comma before “two acres of the site” then splices two independent clauses.

D.why_wrong: “Which was cleared ...” turns the phrase into a relative clause describing “landfill,” but that clause ends at “volunteers,” and “two acres of the site eventually yielded ...” is then joined to the first clause with only a comma.

items.notes: Subject: arts (land art). Band 7: a 14-word past-participle opener that reads naturally as a description of “landfill” (clause 1's last noun) until the subject “two acres of the site” arrives 15 words after the blank; one 46-word run.
band7_moves: S1_period opener of 8 to 30 words that could modify clause 1's last noun

band7.why: 14-word past-participle opener that reads as a description of “landfill” until clause 2’s subject arrives 15 words after the blank; 46-word run; the comma option is the band-7 S1_period trap (0fa289a7, a872c60a).

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses: period before a prepositional opener
items.passage: New Zealand and New Caledonia rise from a vast region of continental crust in the southwestern Pacific, about 94 percent of which lies ______ criteria applied in 2017 by geologist Nick Mortimer and his colleagues, this submerged landmass, known as Zealandia, qualifies as a continent.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “New Zealand and New Caledonia rise from ... about 94 percent of which lies underwater” is a complete sentence. The next sentence opens with the phrase “Under criteria applied in 2017 by geologist Nick Mortimer and his colleagues,” and its subject and verb are “this submerged landmass ... qualifies.” A period correctly separates the two sentences.

B.why_wrong: A comma alone joins two independent clauses: the first ending with “underwater” and the second built around “this submerged landmass ... qualifies.”

C.why_wrong: With no punctuation, “underwater under criteria ...” runs the two sentences together, and the comma before “this submerged landmass” then splices them.

D.why_wrong: “Which” has no verb of its own here, so it leaves the sentence garbled, and “this submerged landmass ... qualifies” is still attached to the first clause with only a comma.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (geology). Band 6: a 12-word prepositional opener before clause 2's subject; clause 1 ends in a which-clause, so the boundary is easy to miss.

fixes: “criteria proposed in 2017” changed to “criteria applied in 2017”: Mortimer and colleagues applied existing continent criteria to Zealandia rather than proposing them

band7.why: 12-word prepositional opener, the band-6 opener type (67667d72 menu); it cannot hang on “underwater”, so the boundary is clear once the subject arrives.

items.subtype: Semicolon before a conjunctive adverb (“instead”) that opens the second clause, comma after it
items.passage: Many ancient engineering projects survive today only as ruins, admired for what they once accomplished. China’s Dujiangyan irrigation system, built in the third century BCE, has not suffered that ______ more than two thousand years after its construction, it still channels water from the Min River to farmland on the Chengdu Plain.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “China’s Dujiangyan irrigation system ... has not suffered that fate” and “more than two thousand years after its construction, it still channels water ...” are both independent clauses. “Instead” opens the second clause, which says what happened in place of that fate, so a semicolon goes before “instead” and a comma after it, setting it off from the introductory phrase that follows.

A.why_wrong: With no punctuation, the two independent clauses (“China’s Dujiangyan irrigation system ... has not suffered that fate” and “it still channels water ...”) run together.

B.why_wrong: A comma alone cannot join two independent clauses; the second clause, “it still channels water ...,” has its own subject and verb.

C.recipe: comma splice (adverb set off by commas)
C.why_wrong: Commas around “instead” treat it as an interrupter, but nothing then separates the two independent clauses, so they are joined with only a comma.

items.notes: Subject: history (ancient engineering). Band 6: a9e5b788 menu (no mark, comma, comma pair around the adverb, semicolon plus adverb); a 7-word phrase after the adverb puts clause 2's subject 9 words past the blank. Rewritten in review: the first version copied 5670a657's frame and option menu.

fixes: rewritten: the first version copied 5670a657’s frame (claim, colon, “X ..., for one. The Y ... is another”) and its option menu; now a9e5b788’s band-6 menu (“fate; instead,”) on the same Dujiangyan subject, Alcántara Bridge dropped
explanation, distractors, subtype, models and notes rewritten to match

band7.why: a9e5b788 band-6 menu after the rewrite; every distractor fails on shape (fused, splice, splice), none on meaning; clause 2’s subject 9 words past the blank.

items.subtype: Conjunctive adverb closing the first clause (contrast with the previous sentence), then a semicolon
items.passage: Many models of planet formation hold that planetesimals, the earliest building blocks of planets, were assembled through violent collisions. Arrokoth, an icy object that NASA’s New Horizons spacecraft flew past in 2019, shows no evidence of such an ______ its two lobes apparently drifted together slowly and merged without significant damage.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “However” contrasts Arrokoth with the models in the previous sentence, so it belongs to the clause “Arrokoth ... shows no evidence of such an origin” and is set off from it by a comma. The semicolon then joins that clause to the next one, “its two lobes apparently drifted together slowly and merged without significant damage,” which explains it rather than contrasting with it.

A.why_wrong: Putting “however” at the start of the second clause sets “its two lobes ... merged without significant damage” against “shows no evidence of such an origin,” but the two statements agree: the slow, gentle merger is why there is no sign of a violent origin.

C.why_wrong: The period is a legal boundary, but “However” would then open the last sentence and set it against the one before, when the last sentence supports it; the contrast belongs with the collision models.

D.why_wrong: Commas around “however” leave two independent clauses (“Arrokoth ... shows no evidence of such an origin” and “its two lobes apparently drifted ...”) joined with only a comma.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (planetary science). Band 7: the adverb closes clause 1 and answers the previous sentence; clause 2 elaborates, so the taught pattern “; however,” and its period variant fail only on meaning (b771d175 menu).
band7_moves: adverb closes clause 1, contrast with the previous sentence

band7.why: Adverb closes clause 1 and answers the previous sentence; “; however,” and “. However,” fail only on meaning; the cue is in another sentence (b771d175, be37d4ae).

items.subtype: Colon after a complete clause ending in a stranded preposition, before the specified item
items.passage: The bronze masks that archaeologists excavated in 1986 at Sanxingdui, a 3,000-year-old site in China’s Sichuan Province, are unlike any other artifacts from that period. The largest has a distinctive feature that few museum visitors fail to comment ______ cylindrical pupils that protrude several inches from the face.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “The largest has a distinctive feature that few museum visitors fail to comment on” is a complete clause; the preposition “on” ends the relative clause. A colon after it correctly introduces the feature itself: “cylindrical pupils that protrude several inches from the face.”

B.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but “cylindrical pupils that protrude ...” is a noun phrase; its verb “protrude” belongs to a relative clause.

C.why_wrong: The period turns “Cylindrical pupils that protrude several inches from the face” into a sentence without a main verb, a fragment.

D.why_wrong: With no punctuation, “comment on cylindrical pupils” runs the noun phrase into the relative clause, which already ends with “on,” and the sentence no longer makes grammatical sense.

items.notes: Subject: history and archaeology (Bronze Age China). Band 6: the clause before the colon ends in a stranded preposition (fba5d8d1 shape), which makes a colon look wrong.

band7.why: Stranded-preposition colon (fba5d8d1 shape); the deciding evidence sits next to the blank.

items.subtype: Colon after a complete clause before a noun phrase that contains a relative clause
items.passage: Franciscan friar Bernardino de Sahagún began documenting Aztec culture in the mid-1500s, intending to help missionaries identify the religious practices they hoped to eradicate. Over decades of work with Nahua scholars and elders, he compiled a record of nearly every aspect of Nahua ______ twelve-book encyclopedia, written in Nahuatl and Spanish, which historians now call the Florentine Codex.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Over decades of work with Nahua scholars and elders, he compiled a record of nearly every aspect of Nahua life” is a complete clause. A colon correctly introduces the noun phrase that says what that record was: “a twelve-book encyclopedia, written in Nahuatl and Spanish, which historians now call the Florentine Codex.”

A.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but “a twelve-book encyclopedia ... which historians now call the Florentine Codex” is a noun phrase; its verb “call” belongs to a relative clause.

B.why_wrong: The period makes “A twelve-book encyclopedia ... which historians now call the Florentine Codex” a sentence of its own, but it has no main verb, so it is a fragment.

C.why_wrong: Adding “it was” turns the noun phrase into an independent clause, which is then joined to the first one with only a comma, a comma splice.

items.notes: Subject: history and literature (colonial Mexico). Band 7: the noun phrase after the colon carries a participle and a relative clause with a finite verb (“which historians now call”), so the period and semicolon options look like they start a clause (e9aee0d8 menu). Clause 1 reworded in review so it no longer echoes e9aee0d8's “something far more extensive.”
band7_moves: noun phrase with a relative clause containing a finite verb after the colon
fragment decoys that look like clauses

fixes: clause 1 reworded (“a work of far greater scope” to “a record of nearly every aspect of Nahua life”) so it no longer echoes e9aee0d8’s “something far more extensive: a”; options, explanation and notes updated

band7.why: Announcing clause plus a noun phrase carrying a participle and a relative clause with a finite verb, so the period and semicolon look like they open a clause (e9aee0d8, f30a478e); the evidence sits inside the 6-word window, as in e9aee0d8.

items.subtype: No punctuation inside a restrictive title plus name; closing comma of the appositive
items.passage: Mhudi, set amid the conflicts of 1830s southern Africa, follows a Barolong couple displaced by warfare. The novel, the only one by journalist and political ______ was published in 1930 and is considered among the earliest English-language novels by a Black South African.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Journalist and political activist” is a title that directly precedes the name “Sol Plaatje,” so no comma separates them. The phrase “the only one by ... Sol Plaatje” interrupts the subject and verb (“The novel ... was published”) and opens with a comma after “novel,” so a matching comma is needed after “Plaatje.”

A.why_wrong: The comma between “activist” and “Sol Plaatje” treats the name as an extra detail, but with no article before it, the title and the name form a single unit.

B.why_wrong: The title and name are correctly joined, but the phrase that opened with a comma after “novel” is never closed before the verb “was published.”

D.recipe: comma intrudes into a unit; missing partner
D.why_wrong: The comma wrongly splits the title from the name, and the phrase opened after “novel” is still left without its closing comma.

items.notes: Subject: literature (South African novel). Band 6: title plus name with a second slot (the closing comma of an appositive opened after “novel”), the 4dcedc31 menu.

band7.why: Title plus name with the closing comma of an appositive opened after “novel” (4dcedc31 menu); nothing after the name tempts a further mark.

items.subtype: Comma plus coordinating conjunction between independent clauses; second clause inverted
items.passage: For generations, the women of Gee’s Bend, Alabama, pieced quilts from discarded work clothes and feed sacks to keep their families ______ only after a 2002 museum exhibition in Houston did the quilts receive widespread recognition as masterpieces of abstract art.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: Both sides of the blank are independent clauses: “the women of Gee’s Bend ... pieced quilts ...” and “only after a 2002 museum exhibition in Houston did the quilts receive widespread recognition ....” The second clause is inverted (“did the quilts receive”), but it is still a main clause, so a comma and the coordinating conjunction “but” join the two.

A.why_wrong: When two long independent clauses are joined by “but,” a comma is conventionally placed before the conjunction.

C.why_wrong: A comma alone cannot join two independent clauses; the inverted clause “only after ... did the quilts receive ...” is not a dependent clause.

D.why_wrong: The two independent clauses run together with no punctuation and no conjunction.

items.notes: Subject: arts (quilting). The plan cell asked for band 7, but S1_comma_conj has no band-7 officials (spec/rw/band7/boundaries.md section 5), so it is written as a strong band 6: clause 2 opens with “only after ...” and an inverted verb, so it looks dependent and the comma alone looks legal.

band7.why: S1_comma_conj has no band-7 official items, so it cannot be band 7; a strong band 6 through the inverted “only after ... did the quilts receive” clause, which looks dependent.

items.subtype: Closing a dash pair around a supplement that contains a parenthesis
items.passage: Brazilian composer Chiquinha Gonzaga wrote polkas, waltzes, and scores for dozens of theatrical productions, but she’s best remembered for a single march. “Ó Abre Alas”—composed in 1899 for a carnival group in Rio de Janeiro (a cordão, or street-parade ______ is often described as the first song written specifically for Brazil’s carnival celebrations.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The dash after “Ó Abre Alas” opens a supplementary element that runs to the end of the parenthesis. The closing parenthesis ends the gloss of “cordão,” and a second dash is then needed to close the element before the verb “is often described.”

A.why_wrong: The supplement was opened with a dash, so it cannot be closed with a comma.

B.why_wrong: A comma inside the parenthesis has no role, and the dash pair is still never closed.

C.why_wrong: The parenthesis is closed, but the element that the dash opened is not, so it runs straight into the verb “is often described.”

items.notes: Subject: arts (music). Band 7: two levels of supplement (a parenthetical gloss with an internal comma inside a dash pair, 83898524 shape); the opening dash is 15 words before the blank.
band7_moves: two levels of supplement in one option
partner mark more than 6 words from the blank

band7.why: Parenthesis with an internal comma inside a dash pair, opening dash 15 words before the blank (83898524 menu); the options differ only in the closing marks, as in 83898524.

items.subtype: Comma before a trailing absolute phrase
items.passage: Rongorongo, a system of glyphs carved into wooden tablets on Rapa Nui (Easter Island), may be one of only a handful of writing systems developed independently. Only about two dozen inscribed artifacts ______ glyphs still undeciphered despite more than a century of attempts by scholars who have compared them with Polynesian chants and astronomical calendars.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Only about two dozen inscribed artifacts survive” is a complete clause. What follows, “their glyphs still undeciphered despite ...,” is an absolute phrase with no main verb of its own (“have compared” belongs to the relative clause “who have compared them”), so a comma correctly attaches it to the clause.

A.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but “their glyphs still undeciphered ...” is a phrase, not a clause.

C.why_wrong: The period makes “Their glyphs still undeciphered despite ...” a sentence without a main verb, a fragment.

D.why_wrong: With no comma, “survive their glyphs” reads as if the artifacts had outlived their own glyphs, and the absolute phrase is not set off from the clause.

items.notes: Subject: language and history (Pacific writing systems). Band 6: absolute phrase whose noun carries a relative clause with a finite verb (“who have compared”), which makes the period and semicolon options look possible (3.24 shape).

band7.why: Absolute phrase after a short clause; the finite verb “have compared” belongs to “scholars” 15 words away, so a local read already settles the comma (the band-7 S2_trailing officials put the finite verb in the trailing phrase’s own head); target was band 6.

items.subtype: Colon between independent clauses; the second, opening with “whereas,” explains the first
items.passage: Traditional gamelan ensembles of Java consist mainly of bronze gongs and metallophones played with mallets. A complete gamelan contains two sets of instruments built to different ______ whereas slendro divides the octave into five roughly equal intervals, pelog divides it into seven unequal ones.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “A complete gamelan contains two sets of instruments built to different tunings” is an independent clause, and so is “pelog divides it into seven unequal ones” (the whereas-clause depends on it). The second explains the first by describing the two tunings, so a colon correctly joins them.

B.why_wrong: The whereas-clause makes the second part look dependent, but its main clause is “pelog divides it into seven unequal ones,” so a comma alone would join two independent clauses.

C.why_wrong: The two independent clauses run together with no punctuation.

D.why_wrong: “And” without a comma does not properly join two long independent clauses, and it presents the description of the tunings as an added fact rather than as the explanation of “different tunings.”

items.notes: Subject: arts (music). Band 7: clause 1 announces (“different tunings”), clause 2 opens with a subordinate whereas-clause so the comma looks legal (9579581e, bb4557cf); the “and” decoy also fails on relation.
band7_moves: cue outside a 6-word window (clause 2's subject 11 words after the blank)

fixes: removed “actually”: it signalled a correction of something sentence 1 never claimed

band7.why: Clause 1 announces, clause 2 opens with a whereas-clause so the comma looks legal; the “and” decoy is also wrong by relation; clause 2’s main subject is 11 words after the blank (9579581e, bb4557cf).

items.subtype: Comma plus coordinating conjunction between independent clauses
items.passage: In a 1990 study at Stanford University, participants tapped out the rhythms of familiar songs, such as “Happy Birthday to You,” while listeners tried to identify each tune. The tappers predicted that the listeners would recognize about half of the ______ the listeners correctly named just three of the 120 songs.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “The tappers predicted that the listeners would recognize about half of the tunes” and “the listeners correctly named just three of the 120 songs” are both independent clauses. A comma followed by the coordinating conjunction “but” correctly joins them and marks the contrast.

A.why_wrong: A comma alone cannot join two independent clauses.

B.why_wrong: When two long independent clauses are joined by “but,” a comma is conventionally placed before the conjunction.

D.why_wrong: The two independent clauses run together with no punctuation and no conjunction.

items.notes: Subject: social science (psychology).

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses: period before a short introductory phrase
items.passage: Nearly 200 pyramids, smaller and more steeply angled than their Egyptian counterparts, occupy the royal cemeteries of Meroë, a capital of the ancient Kingdom of Kush in present-day ______ its height, between approximately 300 BCE and 350 CE, the city was also a major center of iron production.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Nearly 200 pyramids ... occupy the royal cemeteries of Meroë, ... in present-day Sudan” is a complete sentence. The next sentence opens with the phrase “At its height,” and its subject and verb are “the city was.” A period correctly separates the two.

A.why_wrong: A comma alone joins two independent clauses, the second built around “the city was.”

C.why_wrong: With no punctuation, “Sudan at its height” attaches the phrase to the first sentence, and the comma before “the city was” then splices the two clauses.

D.why_wrong: “Which” has no verb of its own, so it leaves the sentence garbled, and “the city was ...” is still attached to the first sentence with only a comma.

items.notes: Subject: history and archaeology (Kingdom of Kush).

items.subtype: Comma before a trailing participial phrase
items.passage: In 2014, the architecture firm The Living built Hy-Fi, a temporary tower in the courtyard of New York’s MoMA PS1 museum. Its bricks were made of chopped corn stalks bound together by fungal ______ allowing the entire structure to be composted rather than thrown away once the summer exhibition ended.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Its bricks were made of chopped corn stalks bound together by fungal mycelium” is a complete clause. The participial phrase “allowing the entire structure to be composted ...” describes a result of that fact and is correctly attached with a comma.

A.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but “allowing the entire structure to be composted ...” is a participial phrase.

B.why_wrong: The period makes “Allowing the entire structure to be composted ...” a sentence without a subject or main verb, a fragment.

C.why_wrong: A colon introduces an explanation, list, or example of what comes before it; the participial phrase states a result, so it should be attached with a comma.

items.notes: Subject: science and technology (biomaterials, architecture).

items.subtype: Closing a comma pair around an interrupting clause
items.passage: Discovered in 1950 near Lake Edward in central Africa, the Ishango bone is a baboon fibula about 20,000 years old. The clusters of notches carved along its length, some researchers ______ represent a rudimentary counting system rather than simple decoration.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Some researchers argue” interrupts the subject (“The clusters of notches carved along its length”) and its verb (“represent”). It opens with a comma after “length,” so a matching comma is needed after “argue.”

B.why_wrong: The interrupter opened with a comma after “length” must also be closed with a comma before the verb “represent.”

C.why_wrong: A semicolon cannot separate a subject from its verb or close an element that opened with a comma.

D.why_wrong: The interrupter opened with a comma, so it cannot be closed with a dash.

items.notes: Subject: history and science (prehistoric mathematics).

fixes: “more than 20,000 years old” softened to “about 20,000 years old”, the usual dating

items.subtype: Closing a dash pair between a subject and its verb
items.passage: Most fast radio bursts originate in distant galaxies, but the one that astronomers detected in April 2020—an intense flash of radio waves lasting a fraction of a ______ was emitted by a magnetar, the extremely dense remnant of a collapsed star, within the Milky Way.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The dash after “2020” opens a supplementary element (“an intense flash of radio waves lasting a fraction of a second”) that describes the burst. A second dash is needed to close it before the verb “was emitted,” which goes with the subject “the one that astronomers detected in April 2020.”

A.why_wrong: The element was opened with a dash, so it cannot be closed with a comma.

B.why_wrong: Without a closing dash, the supplementary element runs straight into the verb “was emitted.”

D.why_wrong: A semicolon cannot separate a subject from its verb, and it cannot close an element that opened with a dash.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (astronomy).

items.subtype: Colon after a complete clause before a list
items.passage: Most soils in the Amazon basin are shallow and nutrient-poor, yet scattered throughout the region are patches of terra preta (“black earth”), a soil so fertile that it’s excavated and sold commercially as potting soil. Archaeologists have determined that these human-made soils share three distinctive ______ fragmented pottery, and food waste.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Archaeologists have determined that these human-made soils share three distinctive components” is a complete clause. A colon correctly introduces the list of those three components: “charcoal, fragmented pottery, and food waste.”

A.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but “charcoal, fragmented pottery, and food waste” is a list, not a clause.

C.why_wrong: The period turns the list “Charcoal, fragmented pottery, and food waste” into a sentence with no verb, a fragment.

D.why_wrong: A colon cannot come between “such as” and the items it introduces; “such as” also wrongly presents the three components as mere examples.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (soil science, archaeology).

items.subtype: No punctuation between a verb and its object
items.passage: In 1966, microbiologist Thomas Brock found a bacterium thriving in a scalding hot spring in Yellowstone National Park. That bacterium, Thermus aquaticus, makes an enzyme that ______ repeated heating used in PCR, a common method for copying DNA.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “The repeated heating used in PCR” is the object of the verb “withstands.” No punctuation should come between a verb and its object.

A.why_wrong: A comma cannot separate the verb “withstands” from its object.

B.why_wrong: A colon cannot come between a verb and its object.

C.why_wrong: The period cuts the verb “withstands” off from its object, and “The repeated heating used in PCR ...” has no main verb.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (microbiology).

items.subtype: No punctuation between a preposition and its object
items.passage: The Venus’ flower basket, a sponge that lives on the deep seafloor of the western Pacific, builds its delicate, cylindrical skeleton ______ silica, the main ingredient in glass. A pair of small shrimp frequently lives inside the sponge, permanently trapped in its latticework.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “From” is a preposition, and “silica” is its object. No punctuation should come between a preposition and its object.

B.why_wrong: A colon cannot separate a preposition from its object.

C.why_wrong: A comma cannot separate a preposition from its object.

D.why_wrong: A single dash has no role between a preposition and its object.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (marine biology).

items.subtype: Direct question: inverted word order and a question mark
items.passage: About 2,000 years ago, the Garamantes cultivated wheat, barley, and grapes in the Sahara Desert, in present-day southwestern Libya, a region that receives almost no rainfall. Where ______ Archaeologists have found the answer underground: hundreds of tunnels that carried groundwater to irrigated fields.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: they got the water for their crops?
did they get the water for their crops.
did they get the water for their crops?
they got the water for their crops.
items.explanation: The sentence that begins with “Where” is a direct question, as the next sentence (“Archaeologists have found the answer”) confirms. A direct question takes question word order (“did they get”) and ends with a question mark.

A.why_wrong: A direct question beginning with “Where” needs question word order (“did they get”), not statement order (“they got”).

B.why_wrong: The word order is right for a direct question, but a direct question must end with a question mark.

D.recipe: direct question left uninverted, ending in a period
D.why_wrong: Statement order and a period leave “Where they got the water for their crops.” as a fragment rather than a question.

items.notes: Subject: history and archaeology (ancient Sahara).

items.subtype: Comma plus coordinating conjunction between independent clauses
items.passage: Guinean scholar Solomana Kanté set out to demonstrate that Manding languages could be written in a script of their own. He completed the N’Ko alphabet in ______ he later used it to write dozens of books on history and traditional medicine.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “He completed the N’Ko alphabet in 1949” and “he later used it to write dozens of books ...” are both independent clauses. A comma followed by the coordinating conjunction “and” correctly joins them.

A.why_wrong: When two independent clauses are joined by “and,” a comma is conventionally placed before the conjunction.

C.why_wrong: A comma alone cannot join two independent clauses.

D.why_wrong: No comma belongs after “and” here; nothing is being set off between the conjunction and “he.”

items.notes: Subject: language (West African writing systems).

items.subtype: Comma after an introductory participial phrase
items.passage: In a 2000 experiment, college students put on an embarrassing T-shirt featuring singer Barry Manilow and entered a classroom full of their peers. Asked afterward how many peers had noticed the ______ the students guessed about half, though only about a quarter had.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Asked afterward how many peers had noticed the shirt” is an introductory participial phrase that describes the subject of the main clause, “the students guessed about half.” A comma correctly separates the introductory phrase from the main clause.

B.why_wrong: A comma is needed to mark where the long introductory phrase ends and the main clause begins; without it, “the shirt the students” runs together.

C.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but “Asked afterward ... the shirt” is a phrase, not a clause.

D.why_wrong: The period turns the phrase “Asked afterward how many peers had noticed the shirt” into a sentence of its own, a fragment with no subject or main verb.

items.notes: Subject: social science (psychology).

items.subtype: Commas between items in a simple series
items.passage: What began in 1956 as a small workshop manufacturing paraffin stoves in Mondragón, a town in Spain’s Basque Country, has grown into one of the world’s largest groups of worker-owned cooperatives. Today the group includes factories, a ______ a university, and a supermarket chain.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Factories,” “a bank,” “a university,” and “a supermarket chain” are items in a simple series. A comma correctly separates “a bank” from the next item, matching the commas elsewhere in the list.

A.recipe: series error (semicolon in a simple list)
A.why_wrong: Semicolons separate list items only when the items themselves contain commas; here the other items are separated by commas.

B.why_wrong: A colon cannot separate one item in a series from the next.

D.why_wrong: Without a comma, “a bank a university” runs two items of the list together.

items.notes: Subject: social science (economics, cooperatives).

items.subtype: Joining two independent clauses: period before a pronoun subject
items.passage: Mudskippers are amphibious fish that spend much of their lives out of water, perched on rocks and mangrove roots. They hop across intertidal mudflats on their muscular front ______ can absorb oxygen through their skin and the lining of their mouths, provided that both stay moist.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “They hop across intertidal mudflats on their muscular front fins” is a complete sentence, and so is “They can absorb oxygen through their skin ....” A period correctly separates the two.

A.why_wrong: A comma alone cannot join two independent clauses.

B.why_wrong: The two independent clauses run together with no punctuation.

C.why_wrong: “And” without a comma does not properly join two independent clauses this long.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (zoology).
